name: Erdős–Anning theorem
statement: Every infinite subset of finite-dimensional real Euclidean space in which each pairwise distance is an integer lies on a straight line.
proof: Erdős' planar proof uses finitely many distance-difference hyperbolas for a noncollinear triple. A dimension-uniform route fixes affinely independent anchors spanning the set. Fix integral distance differences to one anchor, bounded by reverse triangle inequality. Squared distance differences make x affine-linear in the distance to that anchor; its norm equation is quadratic. If the polynomial vanishes identically, its constant term forces the intercept to be the first anchor, and all other anchors lie on the resulting line by equality in Cauchy–Schwarz.
length: 3 pages original or 1 page for short planar proof / 250–500

name: No-trade theorem
statement: Finite-state formulation: at an ex ante Pareto-efficient allocation under a common full-support prior, if a feasible fixed contingent trade is common knowledge to be interim weakly preferred by each trader on an information event, no trader can strictly prefer it at any posterior information atom in that event.

name: Sinkhorn's theorem
statement: For every nonempty finite square real matrix A with all entries >0, there exist positive diagonal D₁,D₂ with D₁AD₂ doubly stochastic. The factors are unique up to reciprocal positive scalars.

name: Midy's theorem
statement: Let b≥2, p prime, 0<a<p, and let the multiplicative order of b mod p be 2k>0. For N=a(b^(2k)−1)/p, the zero-padded length-2k repetend, the two k-digit blocks sum to b^k−1. Equivalently, corresponding digits add to b−1.
proof: Minimality gives b^k≠1 mod p, and b^(2k)=1 implies b^k=−1 mod p. Thus p divides b^k+1. Writing t=a(b^k+1)/p, N=(b^k−1)t=b^k(t−1)+(b^k−t), with 1≤t≤b^k.

name: Multiplication theorem
statement: For integer m≥1 and complex z with Re z>0, ∏_{k=0}^{m−1}Γ(z+k/m)=(2π)^((m−1)/2)m^(1/2−mz)Γ(mz); extend meromorphically away from poles.
proof: For positive real arguments, normalize the product and apply Bohr–Mollerup to its unit recurrence and log-convexity. Evaluate the multiplicative constant by Stirling asymptotics or reflection and sine products, then use analytic continuation.

name: Four-vertex theorem
statement: The curvature of a simple closed C^2 plane curve has at least four local extrema (vertices).
proof: Convex case: with fewer than 4 vertices a line separates arcs of increasing/decreasing curvature; integrate κ' against a linear function for a contradiction.

name: Perpendicular axis theorem
statement: Let μ be any positive mass measure on a Euclidean plane with finite second moment about O. For any orthogonal axes x,y in that plane through O and normal axis z at O, the moments Iₐ=∫dist(p,a)² dμ(p) satisfy I_z=I_x+I_y.
proof: Choose coordinates along the two axes. Pointwise squared distances are y², x² and x²+y². Integrate, using the second moment to infer integrability of each summand.

name: Buckingham π theorem
statement: For positive quantities x∈(ℝ₊)^n with dimension matrix D∈ℝ^(m×n) of rank r, every function invariant under xⱼ↦xⱼ exp((Dᵀu)ⱼ) factors through n−r dimensionless monomials whose exponent vectors form a basis of ker D.
proof: Logs turn unit changes into translations by range Dᵀ. A basis of ker D gives invariant coordinates with exactly those translation fibers.
